title: CI/CD: Continuous Integration & Deployment
blurb: How code actually gets from a commit to production safely, automatically, and repeatedly -- pipelines, deployment strategies, and rollback.
description: Pipelines, automated testing, deployment strategies (rolling, blue-green, canary), rollback, and the operational judgment to ship safely and often.

lessons.title: Why CI/CD exists
objectives: Explain the real problems CI/CD solves, in terms of what manual deployment actually costs a team
Explain how Continuous Integration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Continuous Integration with Continuous Deployment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before CI/CD, deploying code meant a person manually running builds, manually running tests, and manually copying files to a server -- slow, error-prone, and something people naturally avoid doing often (since it's risky and tedious).
examples:
# the vicious cycle CI/CD breaks:
# manual deploys are risky -> teams deploy less often -> each deploy bundles more changes
# -> each deploy becomes even riskier -> teams deploy even LESS often (cycle repeats)
#
# CI/CD's actual fix: make deploying so automated and routine that doing it OFTEN
# is exactly what makes each individual deploy SAFER, not riskier
commonMistakes: Treating CI/CD as just 'automation for its own sake' -- the real point is breaking the cycle where infrequent, risky deploys reinforce each other; frequency and safety are connected, not.
lessons.careerRelevance: Deployment frequency is one of the most cited metrics (alongside lead time, change failure rate, and recovery time) that distinguishes high-performing engineering teams in real industry research.

lessons.title: The anatomy of a pipeline
objectives: Name the typical pipeline stages in order, and explain why order matters
Explain how pipeline stages changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline stages with build and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of automated stages a code change passes through: typically build (compile/package the code), test (run automated tests), and deploy (ship it somewhere) -- often with additional stages like lint (style/quality checks) or security scanning in between.
examples:
# typical stage order, cheapest/fastest checks first:
# lint (seconds) -> build (compile/package) -> test (run automated tests) -> deploy
# if lint fails, the pipeline stops immediately -- no time wasted running build/test/deploy
# on code that already has an obvious style violation
commonMistakes: Running expensive stages before cheap ones -- ordering cheap, fast checks FIRST means failures are caught (and the pipeline stops) as early and cheaply as possible, saving real time on every.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reading and reasoning about a pipeline's stage order (and why a step is placed where it is) is a very common, practical part of working with CI/CD in any real engineering job.

lessons.title: Automated testing in the pipeline
objectives: Explain the test pyramid concept and where each test type typically runs in a pipeline
Explain how test pyramid changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect test pyramid with unit tests and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipelines typically run several LAYERS of automated tests: unit tests (fast, test one small piece in isolation, run on every commit), integration tests (slower, test how pieces work together, e.g. with a real database), and end-to-end tests (slowest, test the whole system as a user would experience it, often run less frequently).
examples:
# the test pyramid, by SPEED and QUANTITY:
# many unit tests (seconds each, run on every commit)
# fewer integration tests (tens of seconds, run on every commit or merge)
# very few end-to-end tests (minutes each, often run before a deploy, not every commit)
commonMistakes: Relying mostly on slow, flaky end-to-end tests instead of a broad base of fast unit tests -- this inverts the test pyramid, making the pipeline slow and unreliable, and is a common.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the same 'Testing' course content applied specifically to CI -- how test types map onto WHEN and HOW OFTEN they run in an automated pipeline.

lessons.title: Build artifacts & versioning
objectives: Explain why you build an artifact ONCE and promote the SAME artifact through environments, rather than rebuilding for each
Explain how build artifact changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect build artifact with build once, promote everywhere and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A build artifact is the packaged, deployable output of the build stage -- a Docker image, a compiled binary, a zip of built assets. A critical, easy-to-miss principle: build the artifact ONCE, then promote that EXACT SAME artifact through dev, staging, and production -- never rebuild separately for each environment.
examples:
# the risk of rebuilding per environment:
# build for staging -> tests pass -> build AGAIN for production (different day, maybe a
# dependency version shifted) -> production artifact is SUBTLY DIFFERENT from what was tested
#
# the fix: build ONCE, tag it (e.g. app:a1b2c3), and promote that EXACT tagged artifact
# through every environment -- what you tested is EXACTLY what ships
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the application separately for each environment -- this breaks the guarantee that what was tested is exactly what gets deployed, reintroducing the very risk automated testing was.
lessons.careerRelevance: "Build once, deploy everywhere" is one of the most consistently emphasized real CI/CD best practices, specifically because violating it has caused real, hard-to-diagnose production incidents.

lessons.title: Environments & promotion
objectives: Explain the typical dev/staging/production environment chain and what 'promotion' means
Explain how environment chain changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment chain with staging and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Most pipelines move a build through a chain of environments with increasing similarity to production and increasing caution: development (fast feedback, may be unstable), staging (a close mirror of production, used for final verification), and production (real users, real consequences).
examples:
# a typical promotion chain:
# dev (fast feedback, engineers verify basic functionality)
# -> staging (mirrors production config/scale, final automated + manual checks)
# -> production (real users -- often gated by an explicit human approval step)
# the SAME artifact moves through all three -- never rebuilt along the way
commonMistakes: Assuming a fully automated pipeline means NO human ever approves a production deploy -- many real, mature CI/CD setups deliberately keep a manual gate before production specifically.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this environment chain and where manual gates typically sit is directly relevant to how release processes are actually structured at most companies.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies
objectives: Distinguish rolling, blue-green, and canary deployment by HOW and WHEN traffic shifts to the new version
Explain how rolling deployment changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect rolling deployment with blue-green deployment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Rolling deployment updates servers gradually, a batch at a time, so both old and new versions run simultaneously during the rollout -- simple and resource-efficient, but a bug only affects the specific servers already updated.
examples:
# the key difference: HOW MUCH traffic sees the new version, and HOW it shifts
# rolling:     gradual server-by-server replacement, no traffic-percentage control
# blue-green:   instant all-or-nothing switch between two full environments
# canary:       fine-grained, gradually-increasing PERCENTAGE of real traffic, watched closely
commonMistakes: Treating all three strategies as interchangeable -- they trade off differently between infrastructure cost, rollback speed, and blast-radius control; the right choice depends on which of.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to explain these three strategies precisely -- not just name them -- is one of the most common, concrete CI/CD questions in real backend and systems interviews.

lessons.title: Feature flags
objectives: Explain how feature flags decouple DEPLOYING code from RELEASING a feature to users
Explain how feature flag changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect feature flag with dark launch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A feature flag is a runtime toggle that controls whether a piece of code path is active, WITHOUT requiring a new deployment to change it. This decouples two things that are often conflated: deploying (the code physically reaches production servers) and releasing (users actually experience the new behavior).
examples:
# decoupling deploy from release:
# deploy new-checkout-flow code with feature_flag('new_checkout') = OFF for everyone
# -- it's IN production, but inactive, causing zero user-facing change
# later: flip the flag to ON for 5% of users, watch metrics, gradually increase --
# all WITHOUT another deployment; a problem means flipping the flag back OFF instantly
commonMistakes: Assuming deploying code and releasing a feature are the same event -- feature flags exist specifically because separating these two lets you deploy far more often (low risk, code is.
lessons.careerRelevance: Feature flags are now a standard practice at nearly every company doing frequent deploys -- directly enabling the 'deploy often, safely' goal this whole course is built around.

lessons.title: Pipeline as code
objectives: Explain why defining a pipeline in a version-controlled config file is preferable to configuring it through a UI
Explain how pipeline as code changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline as code with declarative configuration and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Modern CI/CD pipelines are typically defined in a configuration file (YAML, in tools like GitHub Actions or GitLab CI) that lives in the SAME repository as the code it builds -- 'pipeline as code.' This means pipeline changes go through the same review process as code changes (a pull request).
examples:
# pipeline as code, conceptually (structure varies by tool):
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (or .gitlab-ci.yml) defines:
# stages: [lint, build, test, deploy]
# each stage: what command runs, what triggers it, what it depends on
# this file is REVIEWED and VERSIONED exactly like any other code change
commonMistakes: Configuring a pipeline entirely through a CI tool's UI, with no config file in the repository -- this leaves the pipeline definition un-reviewed, unversioned, and disconnected from the code.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reading and editing a YAML pipeline config is one of the most immediately practical, everyday CI/CD skills expected in real backend and DevOps-adjacent roles.

lessons.title: Secrets & security in CI/CD
objectives: Explain why secrets must never appear in pipeline config files or logs, and how CI systems handle them safely instead
Explain how secrets management changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect secrets management with environment variables and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipelines often need secrets -- API keys, database passwords, deployment credentials -- to do their job, but these must NEVER be hard-coded directly into a pipeline config file (which is version-controlled, often visible to many people, and preserved in history forever, even if later 'removed').
examples:
# what goes wrong, and the fix:
# WRONG: api_key = 'sk_live_abc123' committed directly in the pipeline YAML file
# (now permanently in git history, visible to anyone with repo access, forever)
# RIGHT: api_key = ${{ secrets.API_KEY }} -- injected at runtime from the CI
# platform's secrets store, and automatically masked if it appears in log output
commonMistakes: Printing a full configuration or environment object for debugging without checking whether it contains secrets -- this is a genuinely common, real way secrets leak into logs even when they.
lessons.careerRelevance: Secrets accidentally committed to a public repository is one of the most common real security incidents in the industry -- directly connects this lesson to the earlier Cybersecurity course.

lessons.title: Caching & pipeline speed
objectives: Explain what a pipeline typically caches, and why pipeline speed matters beyond just convenience
Explain how dependency caching changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect dependency caching with build cache and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipelines commonly cache dependency downloads (e.g. installed packages) and build intermediates between runs, since redownloading and rebuilding unchanged dependencies on every single run wastes real time -- often the majority of a build's total duration.
examples:
# a common caching win:
# without cache: every run re-downloads and reinstalls ALL dependencies from scratch (~2 min)
# with cache: dependencies unchanged since last run -> restore from cache (~5 sec)
# multiplied across dozens of runs per day, this is a genuinely large time savings
commonMistakes: Treating pipeline speed as a minor convenience rather than something that actively shapes team behavior -- a slow pipeline discourages exactly the frequent, small commits that make.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pipeline execution time is a real, tracked metric at most engineering organizations, precisely because of its direct effect on how often engineers are willing to integrate and ship.

lessons.title: GitOps
objectives: Explain the core GitOps idea: Git as the single source of truth for desired system state
Explain how GitOps changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GitOps with declarative desired state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: GitOps takes the 'pipeline as code' idea further: the DESIRED STATE of an entire deployed system (which version is running, how many replicas, configuration values) is described declaratively in a Git repository, and an automated controller continuously works to make the ACTUAL running system match what's in Git.
examples:
# the GitOps loop, conceptually:
# 1. Git repo says: 'app should be running version v3, with 5 replicas'
# 2. a controller (e.g. ArgoCD, Flux) continuously compares this to the ACTUAL running state
# 3. if they differ, the controller automatically applies changes to match Git
# every production change traces back to a specific, reviewed Git commit
commonMistakes: Confusing GitOps with 'just using Git for CI/CD pipeline config' -- GitOps specifically means Git describes the DESIRED RUNNING STATE of the system, with an automated controller actively.
lessons.careerRelevance: GitOps (via tools like ArgoCD or Flux) is an increasingly common practice specifically in Kubernetes-based deployments, connecting directly to the earlier Kubernetes course.

lessons.title: Diagnosing a broken pipeline
objectives: Recognize the most common categories of pipeline failure and where to look for each
Explain how pipeline failure categories changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline failure categories with environment mismatch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipeline failures tend to fall into recognizable categories: a genuine code or test failure (the pipeline is correctly catching a real problem -- read the actual error message first); an environment mismatch (works locally, fails in CI, often due to a missing dependency or different tool version between environments).
examples:
# diagnosing by SYMPTOM pattern:
# 'fails every single time, same error' -> likely a real code/test failure -- read the actual message
# 'works on my machine, fails in CI' -> likely an environment mismatch (versions, missing deps)
# 'fails sometimes, no code changed, different failure each time' -> likely a flaky test
# 'CI itself won't even start, or times out with no useful output' -> likely infrastructure
commonMistakes: Assuming every pipeline failure is a real bug in the code being tested -- correctly recognizing flaky tests and environment/infrastructure issues as DIFFERENT categories, with different.
lessons.careerRelevance: This pattern-based diagnosis mirrors the earlier Debugging course's own philosophy, applied specifically to the unique failure modes a CI/CD pipeline introduces.

quiz.q: What vicious cycle does CI/CD break?
options: Too much testing
Manual deploys are risky, so teams deploy less often, so each deploy bundles more changes and becomes riskier
Too many engineers
Slow internet connections

quiz.q: Why does pipeline stage order matter?
options: It doesn't matter at all
Cheaper/faster checks should run first so failures are caught before wasting time on expensive stages
Stages must run in alphabetical order
Later stages always run faster

quiz.q: What real problem does Continuous Integration solve?
options: Slow internet
'Integration hell' from long-lived branches with large, painful merges
Too many unit tests
Expensive cloud bills

quiz.q: What does the test pyramid recommend?
options: Equal numbers of every test type
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end tests
Only end-to-end tests
No automated tests, only manual QA

quiz.q: Why should you build an artifact once and promote it, rather than rebuilding per environment?
options: Rebuilding is against best practice for no reason
Rebuilding risks the artifact tested in staging being subtly different from what reaches production
Rebuilding is always faster
It reduces the number of environments needed

quiz.q: What is a common reason a manual approval gate exists before production, even in an automated pipeline?
options: Automation is broken
A deliberate human decision point before affecting real users is a common, intentional safety practice
It's required by law everywhere
It makes the pipeline faster

quiz.q: What distinguishes blue-green deployment from rolling deployment?
options: They are identical
Blue-green switches ALL traffic instantly between two full environments; rolling updates gradually, batch by batch
Blue-green is always slower
Rolling deployment requires double the infrastructure

quiz.q: What does canary deployment specifically control?
options: Database schema changes
A gradually-increasing percentage of real traffic routed to the new version
The programming language used
The build cache

quiz.q: What do feature flags decouple?
options: Frontend and backend code
Deploying code (reaching production) from releasing a feature (users experiencing it)
Git branches from each other
Testing from deployment

quiz.q: What is the benefit of 'pipeline as code' (a version-controlled config file)?
options: It makes builds faster
Pipeline changes go through the same review process as code, and are versioned alongside it
It removes the need for testing
It requires no configuration at all

quiz.q: Where should secrets like API keys live in a pipeline?
options: Hard-coded directly in the pipeline YAML file
In a secrets store, injected as environment variables at runtime and masked in logs
In a public comment for documentation
In the commit message

quiz.q: What does pipeline caching typically speed up?
options: The programming language itself
Dependency downloads and build intermediates that haven't changed since the last run
Network latency to users
Database queries

quiz.q: Why can a code-only rollback sometimes fail?
options: Rollbacks never fail
If a bad deploy included an incompatible database migration, old code may not work against the new schema
Rollbacks are always instant
Old code is always compatible with any schema

quiz.q: What is the core idea behind GitOps?
options: Using Git for version control only
Git describes the desired system state, and a controller continuously reconciles the actual running system to match it
Storing secrets in Git
Writing pipeline YAML files

quiz.q: Why is correctly categorizing a pipeline failure (real bug vs flaky test vs infrastructure) important?
options: It isn't important
Debugging a flaky test as if it were a real code bug wastes effort chasing a problem that isn't actually there
All pipeline failures are the same
It only matters for large teams

quiz.q: What symptom typically suggests a flaky test rather than a real bug?
options: It fails every single time with the same error
It fails intermittently with no code change, often a different failure each time
It never fails
It only happens in production

quiz.q: What's the underlying goal connecting every practice in this course?
options: Using as many tools as possible
Making it safe to ship small, frequent changes rather than large, infrequent ones
Avoiding all automation
Maximizing the number of environments

quiz.q: Why doesn't automating deploys alone make a system safer?
options: Automation always makes things safer regardless
Automation without automated testing just makes it faster to ship a broken change
Automation is unrelated to safety
Automated deploys are always slower

quiz.q: What's a genuinely common way secrets leak even when stored correctly in a secrets manager?
options: They never leak once stored correctly
Printing a full config or environment object for debugging, without checking whether it contains the secret
Secrets managers are inherently insecure
Only through direct hacking

quiz.q: Why is a slow pipeline a real problem, not just an inconvenience?
options: It has no real effect on team behavior
It discourages the frequent, small commits that Continuous Integration depends on working well
Slow pipelines are always more secure
It only affects cloud costs

exercises.title: Order pipeline stages by cost
exercises.prompt: Given lint (5s), unit tests (30s), integration tests (3min), and deploy -- what's the correct fail-fast order, and why?
exercises.hint: lint -> unit tests -> integration tests -> deploy; cheapest and fastest checks run first so a failure is caught before wasting time on expensive later stages

exercises.title: Diagnose integration hell
exercises.prompt: A team merges feature branches only once every 3 weeks, and merges routinely take a full day to resolve. What CI practice would most directly address this, and why?
exercises.hint: trunk-based development / frequent small merges (Continuous Integration) -- integrating in small, frequent increments keeps conflicts small and recent instead of large and stale

exercises.title: Rebalance an inverted test pyramid
exercises.prompt: A pipeline has 500 slow, flaky end-to-end tests and only 20 unit tests. What's wrong with this shape, and what would you recommend?
exercises.hint: this is an inverted test pyramid -- recommend building out a much larger base of fast, reliable unit tests, and trimming e2e tests down to cover only genuinely critical user flows

exercises.title: Spot a build-once violation
exercises.prompt: A team rebuilds their Docker image separately for staging and production, using the same Dockerfile but run on different days. What real risk does this introduce?
exercises.hint: the artifact tested in staging may not be byte-for-byte identical to what deploys to production (e.g. a dependency version could shift between builds) -- violates build-once-promote-everywhere

exercises.title: Decide where a manual gate belongs
exercises.prompt: In a dev -> staging -> production pipeline, where would you place a manual approval gate, and why there specifically?
exercises.hint: before production specifically -- a deliberate human decision point right before affecting real users, even in an otherwise fully automated pipeline

exercises.title: Choose a deployment strategy
exercises.prompt: A team wants to catch a bad deploy while it affects only a small fraction of real users, gradually increasing exposure. Which strategy fits, and why not blue-green?
exercises.hint: canary deployment -- fine-grained, gradually-increasing traffic percentage; blue-green switches ALL traffic at once, so it wouldn't limit exposure to a small fraction first

exercises.title: Trace a rolling deployment
exercises.prompt: 4 servers, batch size 2. After the first batch completes, what does the server-version state look like?
exercises.hint: 2 servers on the new version, 2 still on the old version -- both versions serving traffic simultaneously mid-rollout

exercises.title: Design a feature-flag rollout
exercises.prompt: You want to ship a risky new checkout flow. Describe how you'd use a feature flag to deploy it safely well before it's fully tested.
exercises.hint: deploy the code with the flag OFF for everyone (dark launch) -- it's in production but inactive; later flip it on for a small percentage, watch metrics, then gradually increase, all without another deploy

exercises.title: Explain pipeline-as-code's review benefit
exercises.prompt: A pipeline is configured entirely through a CI tool's UI, with no YAML file in the repo. What real problem does this create?
exercises.hint: pipeline changes aren't reviewed like code changes and aren't versioned alongside the code history -- there's no pull request, no diff, no way to see what the pipeline looked like for an old commit

exercises.title: Fix a secrets leak
exercises.prompt: A pipeline YAML file contains the line `api_key: 'sk_live_abc123'` directly. What's wrong, and what's the fix?
exercises.hint: the secret is hard-coded in a version-controlled file, permanently in git history and visible to anyone with repo access; fix by moving it to the CI platform's secrets store and referencing it as an injected environment variable

exercises.title: Explain a caching win
exercises.prompt: A build takes 2 minutes without caching (re-downloading all dependencies) and 5 seconds with a warm cache. Why does this matter beyond convenience?
exercises.hint: a slow pipeline discourages the frequent, small commits Continuous Integration depends on -- caching keeps the feedback loop fast enough that engineers don't avoid running the pipeline often

exercises.title: Diagnose a rollback that isn't actually safe
exercises.prompt: A deploy renamed a database column from `name` to `full_name`. The new code has a bug, so the team rolls back to the OLD code. What goes wrong?
exercises.hint: the old code expects a column called `name`, which no longer exists after the migration -- a code-only rollback breaks against the already-migrated schema; migrations need to be backward-compatible for this to work safely

exercises.title: Explain the GitOps reconciliation loop
exercises.prompt: In a GitOps setup, a team wants to scale a service from 3 to 5 replicas. What do they actually change, and what happens next?
exercises.hint: they change the desired replica count in the Git repository (not the live cluster directly); a controller detects the difference between desired (5) and actual (3) state and applies the change automatically

exercises.title: Categorize a pipeline failure
exercises.prompt: A test fails intermittently, with a different error each time, and no code has changed recently. What category of failure is this most likely, and what would you check?
exercises.hint: likely a flaky test -- check for timing assumptions, shared state between tests, or reliance on external services that aren't properly mocked/isolated

exercises.title: Diagnose 'works on my machine'
exercises.prompt: A test passes locally but fails in CI with no code changes. What category of issue is this, and what's a likely specific cause?
exercises.hint: an environment mismatch -- likely causes include a different dependency or language/tool version installed in CI versus locally, or a missing environment variable/config that exists locally but not in CI

exercises.title: Combine deployment strategy with feature flags
exercises.prompt: A team is deploying via canary (10% of traffic) AND the new code is behind a feature flag defaulting to off. Explain why combining both gives even finer control than either alone.
exercises.hint: canary controls WHICH SERVERS run the new code; the feature flag controls WHETHER the new behavior is even active once running -- combining both means you can deploy broadly but activate the risky behavior even more narrowly and independently

exercises.title: Justify a manual gate against 'full automation'
exercises.prompt: A colleague argues a truly mature CI/CD pipeline should have zero manual steps, including before production. How would you respond, using this course's own framing?
exercises.hint: a deliberate manual approval gate before production is a common, intentional safety practice even in mature pipelines -- full automation and human oversight aren't opposed; the goal is safe frequent shipping, not the complete absence of any human judgment

exercises.title: Trace the full 'ship safely and often' chain
exercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, how CI (small changes), automated testing, a deployment strategy, and feature flags work TOGETHER (not just individually) to make frequent shipping safe.
exercises.hint: CI keeps each change small; automated testing catches problems before users see them; the deployment strategy limits how many users a bad change affects if it slips through; feature flags let you decouple deploying from activating a risky change -- each layer catches what the others might miss

projects.desc: Design a lint -> build -> test -> deploy pipeline for a simple app, explaining the order and what each stage checks.

projects.title: Simulate a canary rollout with a rollback trigger
projects.desc: Design a canary deployment plan with specific metrics that would trigger an automatic rollback if the new version underperforms.

projects.title: Add feature flags to a risky feature rollout

interviewPreparation.q: Explain the difference between rolling, blue-green, and canary deployment strategies.
interviewPreparation.a: Rolling deployment updates servers gradually in batches, so old and new versions run simultaneously during rollout. Blue-green keeps two complete environments and switches all traffic instantly once the new one is verified, enabling fast rollback at the cost of double infrastructure. Canary routes a small, gradually-increasing percentage of real traffic to the new version, catching problems while they only affect a small fraction of users.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is 'build once, promote everywhere' an important CI/CD principle?
interviewPreparation.a: If you rebuild separately for each environment, any non-determinism in the build process (a dependency version shifting, a different build-time variable) means the artifact tested in staging might not be identical to what actually reaches production. Building once and promoting that exact artifact through every environment guarantees what was tested is exactly what ships.

interviewPreparation.q: Why can a rollback sometimes fail even when you redeploy the exact previous code?
interviewPreparation.a: If the bad deploy included a database migration (e.g. renaming a column), the old code may not be compatible with the new schema -- rollback safety requires the schema change itself to be backward-compatible for at least one release cycle, not just having the old code available to redeploy.

interviewPreparation.q: What do feature flags actually decouple, and why does that matter?
interviewPreparation.a: They decouple deploying code (physically reaching production) from releasing a feature (users actually experiencing it). This lets teams deploy code far more often -- even incomplete work, behind a flag defaulting to off -- while controlling exactly when and to whom a feature activates, independent of any deployment.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the real difference between a genuine test failure, a flaky test, and an environment mismatch in a broken pipeline, and why does correctly categorizing it matter?
interviewPreparation.a: A genuine failure fails consistently and indicates a real problem in the code. A flaky test fails intermittently with no code change, often from timing or shared-state issues. An environment mismatch works locally but fails in CI due to version or configuration differences. Correctly categorizing which one you're facing matters because debugging a flaky test as if it were a real code bug wastes significant time chasing a problem that isn't actually in the code.

capstone.title: Design a Complete, Safe Shipping Pipeline
capstone.description: Design an end-to-end CI/CD pipeline for a realistic application: define every stage from commit to production, choose and justify a deployment strategy, incorporate feature flags for at least one risky feature, and explicitly design for rollback safety including a database migration scenario.
deliverables: A full pipeline diagram: every stage from commit to production, in the correct fail-fast order
A chosen deployment strategy (rolling, blue-green, or canary) with a specific, honest justification tied to this system's actual constraints -- not just 'this is the modern choice'
A feature-flag plan for at least one risky feature, from dark launch through full rollout
A rollback plan that explicitly addresses a database migration scenario, showing how backward compatibility is preserved for one release cycle
A short section identifying at least 2 likely pipeline failure categories for this system and how you'd diagnose each
capstone.portfolioTips: The deployment-strategy justification is the most revealing part of this capstone -- explaining WHY a strategy fits your system's specific constraints (not just naming it) is exactly the depth real system-design interviews are testing for.
